ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> The hypotheses are then tested using a between-group design where participants are asked to either lie or tell the truth about a certain event or topic (e.g., what they did at the weekend).

> Positive values on the y-axis mean that participants provided longer statements when they lied compared to when they told the truth.

> In this hypothetical study, participants were required to tell both truths and lies.

> In each trial participants are presented with a prompt-a word or phrase-and are required to briefly describe the first memory they recall in response to the prompt.

> Participants are divided into pairs.

> Participants are to discuss each topic together for approximately one minute.

> For each trial, participants are randomly assigned to either discuss the topic honestly or deceitfully.

> Even in studies in which the same participants are assessed several times (as is the case in the data we examined above), conventional statistical approaches still do not provide insights on the individual level.

> Notably, these participants had quite different individual-level cues to deception.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. How can you tell when someone is lying?
This question has fascinated humans for millennia and empirical psychologists for over a century (Denault et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This question has fascinated humans for millennia and empirical psychologists for over a century <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Denault et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Central to psychological research on the topic is the development and assessment of causal theories to explain what cues-behavioral indicators-can be used to distinguish lies from truths.

However, despite the many proposed theories and the extensive empirical work on deception cues, we are still far from a satisfying answering to the fundamental question of how to tell when someone is lying.

The reason is that all theories of deception detection assume causal explanations at the level of the individual, yet almost all research on deception cues compares the behavior when lying or telling the truth at the group level.
At first glance, this preference for group-level research may seem inconsequential.
However, translating group-level findings to individual-level explanations is not as straightforward as one might think.

Unless two conditions are met, described by the mathematical theorems of ergodicity, one cannot extrapolate findings on the group level to the individual level (Molenaar, 2004; Molenaar & Campbell, 2009).
text.formatted: Unless two conditions are met, described by the mathematical theorems of ergodicity, one cannot extrapolate findings on the group level to the individual level <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Molenaar, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Molenaar & Campbell, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: We will show that these conditions are not met for deception cues.
Consequently, deception researchers' near exclusive use of group-level methodology says little about the underlying theories they are purporting to test.
Rather, to appropriately test theories of deception cues, a wholly different, individuallevel, research paradigm is required.
Our aim with this article is to sketch a way forward to establish this new individuallevel approach to deception cue research.
We begin by providing a non-technical description of the ergodic theorems and explain the limitations of using group-level research to test causal theories in psychology.
We then discuss the implications of this for deception research and explain why the field needs an individual-level research agenda.
Finally, we offer tractable steps towards this goal by outlining an individual level research agenda to deception cue research.
Several of the issues we raise regarding the problem of using group-level methodologies in deception research apply to many areas of psychology.
For discussions on the broader implications of group-level methodologies for psychological research see Molenaar (2004), Molenaar and Campbell (2009), and Speelman and McGann (2026).
text.formatted: For discussions on the broader implications of group-level methodologies for psychological research see <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Molenaar (2004)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Molenaar and Campbell (2009)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Speelman and McGann (2026)</ref>.

text.text: Here we zero in on deception research, using it as a case study to illustrate the broader implications discussed elsewhere.
In doing so, we aim to show the limitations of group-level research and the opportunities of complementing group-level research with individual-level methodologies.
We focus on deception cue research because we believe group-level methodologies are particularly problematic in this field of enquiry.

First, deception cues are likely highly sensitive to context (Markowitz & Hancock, 2019) and individual differences (e.g., Lane et al, 2014), complicating how group-level findings should be interpreted on the individual level.
text.formatted: First, deception cues are likely highly sensitive to context <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Markowitz & Hancock, 2019)</ref> and individual differences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lane et al, 2014)</ref>, complicating how group-level findings should be interpreted on the individual level.

text.text: Second, decades of group-level research has failed to provide compelling tests of the underlying theoretical mechanisms posited as the causes of deception cues.
It is, therefore, unsurprising that there is considerable disagreement between deception researchers on the validity of deception theories (Luke et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It is, therefore, unsurprising that there is considerable disagreement between deception researchers on the validity of deception theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Luke et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this paper, we argue that to move the field forward, a change of tack is required, and encourage researchers to adopt an individual-level approach to research on deception cues.
Research conducted at the group level focuses on interindividual variation.
That is, differences between individuals.
However, most psychological processes and causal theories are at the level of the individual, focusing on intraindividual variation-how individuals vary over time.
In Figure 1, this distinction is schematically demonstrated using a Cattell Box (Cattell, 1952).
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, this distinction is schematically demonstrated using a Cattell Box <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cattell, 1952)</ref>.

text.text: The blue vertical slice represents a typical group-level study, where several individuals are measured on one occasion.
The horizontal red slice represents an individuallevel study, where the same individual is measured on several occasions.
A model or a process is said to be ergodic when one can apply quantitative conclusions on the group level to the individual level, or vice versa.
For a process to be ergodic, two conditions must be met (Molenaar, 2004; Molenaar & Campbell, 2009): Condition 1.
text.formatted: For a process to be ergodic, two conditions must be met <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Molenaar, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Molenaar & Campbell, 2009)</ref>: Condition 1.

text.text: Homogeneity across individuals: Ergodicity requires that each subject in the population must follow the same statistical model.
As an example, consider a test of cognitive ability designed to measure a single latent factor of intelligence, in addition to two subfactors, verbal and numerical intelligence.
To extrapolate from the group to the individual, this hierarchical factor structure and loadings must be identical for each subject in a population.
If, for some individuals, the factor structure of their test responses differs from the group-level structure, Condition 1 would not be met.
Ergodicity requires that statistical models should be stationary across occasions; they should not vary over time or across settings.
Developmental processes, learning, and habituation are examples of psychological processes that vary over time and therefore would not fulfill Condition 2.
Consider for instance how one can get used to a bad smell.
How well your rating will match a group's average rating for how bad a smell is will depend on how long you have been exposed to it.
Such habituation processes are non-ergodic: Different models are required to describe an individual's experience and the group average.
When both Condition 1 and 2 are met, a process is ergodic, and one can directly draw inferences about the individual-level from findings at the group-level (and vice versa).
An example of psychological processes that are reasonably ergodic are the gestalt principles of perception (Wertheimer, 1938).
text.formatted: An example of psychological processes that are reasonably ergodic are the gestalt principles of perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Wertheimer, 1938)</ref>.

text.text: These principles are relatively stable across individuals and across time (though even the gestalt principles show some maturation effects; Furth & Mendez, 1963).
text.formatted: These principles are relatively stable across individuals and across time (though even the gestalt principles show some maturation effects; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Furth & Mendez, 1963)</ref>.

text.text: However, when one or both conditions are not met, a process is non-ergodic.
In such situations, one cannot make valid inferences to the individual-level from research conducted at the group-level.
This limitation has important consequences for the testing of psychological theories.

If the theory to be tested functions at the level of the individual, and if the underlying process is non-ergodic, then group-level research is an inappropriate way to examine the proposed causal-mechanisms of the theory (Speelman & McGann, 2026).
text.formatted: If the theory to be tested functions at the level of the individual, and if the underlying process is non-ergodic, then group-level research is an inappropriate way to examine the proposed causal-mechanisms of the theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Speelman & McGann, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The error of conducting group-level research in such contexts is all too common in psychology. Speelman and McGann (2026) explain how this ultimately concerns issues around group aggregation.
text.formatted: The error of conducting group-level research in such contexts is all too common in psychology. <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Speelman and McGann (2026)</ref> explain how this ultimately concerns issues around group aggregation.

text.text: The logic behind group-level research is that by averaging across large samples, thereby accounting for random error and individual differences, researchers can get better estimates of the underlying psychological processes.
However, this logic only holds if all individuals being tested follow the same underlying psychological process.

If individuals in a group follow qualitatively different processes, aggregation becomes highly problematic and may say little or nothing about how the process works on an individual level. Mehoudar et al.'s (2014) study on the eye tracking patterns of facial processing provides a concrete example.
text.formatted: If individuals in a group follow qualitatively different processes, aggregation becomes highly problematic and may say little or nothing about how the process works on an individual level. <ref type="bibr">Mehoudar et al.'s (2014)</ref> study on the eye tracking patterns of facial processing provides a concrete example.

text.text: On a group-level Mehoudar et al. replicated the well-known triangular shape pattern of facial processing, where an increase in fixations is shown for the areas around the eyes and nose (Althoff & Cohen, 1999 ; Yarbus, 1967).
text.formatted: On a group-level Mehoudar et al. replicated the well-known triangular shape pattern of facial processing, where an increase in fixations is shown for the areas around the eyes and nose <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Althoff & Cohen, 1999 ;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Yarbus, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: However, on the individual-level, people showed a diverse set of unique, yet stable, scanning patterns, that were largely inconsistent with the triangular shape observed when aggregating the data.
This strongly indicates that these individuals were using qualitatively different strategies for the task of facial processing.
This crucial finding could not have been discovered when using grouplevel data (Speelman and McGann, 2026).
text.formatted: This crucial finding could not have been discovered when using grouplevel data <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Speelman and McGann, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Examining theory and data in the deception literature, it is clear that deception research has also committed the error of conducting grouplevel research to test individual-level processes.
All causal theories of deception cues (that is, theories about how and why cues to deception should manifest) function at the level of the individual.

Consider the popular cognitive load theory, which holds that lying is more cognitively demanding than truth telling, and that this can result in reliable deception cues such as delayed response times (Sporer, 2016).
text.formatted: Consider the popular cognitive load theory, which holds that lying is more cognitively demanding than truth telling, and that this can result in reliable deception cues such as delayed response times <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Sporer, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Since cognitive load is a psychological process that occurs at the level of the individual, the causal explanation for this theory must also be at the individual level.

The same applies to all deception theories, regardless of whether they focus on emotion (Ekman et al., 1988), arousal (de Turck & Miller, 1985), self-presentation (DePaulo et al., 2003), or any other mechanism.
text.formatted: The same applies to all deception theories, regardless of whether they focus on emotion <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ekman et al., 1988)</ref>, arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(de Turck & Miller, 1985)</ref>, self-presentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(DePaulo et al., 2003)</ref>, or any other mechanism.

text.text: The underpinning psychological processes of all such theories occur at the individual level.
On the other hand, the methodological paradigm that has dominated research on deception detection compares the behaviors of people telling the truth or lying at the group level.

In a typical study, hypotheses (e.g., lies will be shorter than true statements) are derived from some explanatory mechanism at the individual level (e.g., fabricating is more cognitively demanding than remembering).
The hypotheses are then tested using a between-group design where participants are asked to either lie or tell the truth about a certain event or topic (e.g., what they did at the weekend).
Their behavior or statement is then coded on some cue of interest (e.g., statement length).
The average degree to which this cue manifests when providing honest compared to deceptive statements is then compared.
As noted above, an implicit assumption of this group-level approach is that all participants follow the same underlying psychological process (Speelman & McGann, 2026).
text.formatted: As noted above, an implicit assumption of this group-level approach is that all participants follow the same underlying psychological process <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Speelman & McGann, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In our example, this would mean that all people tested find remembering easier than fabrication (and at an identical magnitude) and that ease of production can be accurately measured by statement length.

However, if some people follow a qualitatively different process (e.g., if some people find fabricating easier than remembering or if people find fabrication difficult to varying extents), any observed difference in group means will not be indicative of individual level patterns.

A similar problem occurs if the process changes on different occasions or in different settings relevant to the hypothesis being tested (e.g., under some circumstances, fabrication is easier than remembering, and under other circumstances, the opposite is true).
Thus, if either issue occurs, a between-subjects comparison such as this will not provide a test of the individual-level explanations underpinning the hypotheses of the study 1 .

This problem should not be understated: If one posits a substantive hypothesis about individual-level mechanisms, one cannot test this hypothesis with group-level data unless the assumption of ergodicity holds.
Again, for group-level research to say something meaningful about individual-level processes, the two aforementioned conditions for ergodicity must be met.
In the following section we show how untenable this claim is for deception cues.
Many (if not most) psychological processes would fail to meet both conditions required for ergodicity.
Deception cues are no exception.
The potential influence of temporal effects and individual differences on deception cues is simply too great for them to be ergodic.
To illustrate this, consider the deception cue statement detail-one of the most studied deception cues (DePaulo et al., 2003; Vrij et al., 2017).
text.formatted: To illustrate this, consider the deception cue statement detail-one of the most studied deception cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(DePaulo et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Vrij et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, detail refers to how much granular information a person includes in their verbal statement.
The statistical model typically used to characterize this cue (and most cues in the literature) is simply a (standardized) mean difference in detail between truthful and deceptive messages.
Past research often finds that deceptive statements are less detailed than truthful statements at the group level (Amado et al., 2016; DePaulo et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Past research often finds that deceptive statements are less detailed than truthful statements at the group level <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amado et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">DePaulo et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: It is also useful to view mean differences through the framework of the general linear model.
In this framework, such a mean difference is the slope in a regression model for a predictor representing veracity.
Implied by the model is an intercept representing the mean level of detail (for truths, lies, or collapsed across both depending on how the veracity indicator is coded).
Ergodicity requires that the slope and intercept of this model apply homogeneously across people and stationarily across occasions.

Thus, if we hypothesize that detail as a cue to deception is ergodic, the following would need to be true: All individuals give statements that are less detailed when lying, deviating from the same baseline with the same average magnitude (Condition 1) each time they tell a lie (Condition 2).
This hypothesis of ergodicity seems implausible on its face, both on the basis of theoretical reasoning about the likely psychological processes involved and on the basis of data.

For example, ergodicity would implicitly assume that all people are equally (un)able to generate sufficient compelling detail when they fabricate a story, but people likely vary widely in this capacity (Nahari & Pazuelo, 2015; Nahari & Vrij, 2014).
text.formatted: For example, ergodicity would implicitly assume that all people are equally (un)able to generate sufficient compelling detail when they fabricate a story, but people likely vary widely in this capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Nahari & Pazuelo, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Nahari & Vrij, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond reasoning about the plausibility of ergodicity, we can examine data from past studies to empirically assess whether the requirements are met.
We stress that these analyses are not meant as a criticism of the studies from which the data has been taken or the researchers who have done the good work of collecting these data.
Rather, they are simply used to further examine our claim that deception cues are non-ergodic.
In all cases except Luke (2015), the analyses reported here do not address the same statistical hypotheses examined in the original studies.
text.formatted: In all cases except <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Luke (2015)</ref>, the analyses reported here do not address the same statistical hypotheses examined in the original studies.

text.text: Code to reproduce the analyses and visualizations reported here, as well as full-size image files for the figures, can be found at https://osf.io/62pgy/?view_only=a659cd7ca5a04dc0bdd1de77adb33cd2.

text.text: In one relevant experiment, Warmelink and O'Connell (2023) coded the number of details provided by people as they lied or told the truth during an interview (N = 99).
text.formatted: In one relevant experiment, <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Warmelink and O'Connell (2023)</ref> coded the number of details provided by people as they lied or told the truth during an interview (N = 99).

text.text: They coded each person's responses to each of seven interview questions, which can be treated as separate occasions for the purpose of assessing the stationarity requirement (Condition 2).
Using the data from this experiment, we calculated a standardized mean difference (Hedge's g) between truthful and deceptive statements for each question.
The effects ranged from g = 0.49 to g = -0.38, and there was significant heterogeneity for the differences across occasions, Q (5) = 17.35, p = .004.
For some questions, truths were more detailed than lies, and for others, lies were more detailed than truths.
These results indicate that in this dataset the stationarity requirement is not met for this purported cue to deception.

In another experiment, Luke (2015) coded the number of details provided in an interview by participants (N = 99), all of whom told the truth about some of their activities and some of whom also lied about some activities.
text.formatted: In another experiment, <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Luke (2015)</ref> coded the number of details provided in an interview by participants (N = 99), all of whom told the truth about some of their activities and some of whom also lied about some activities.

text.text: The data from this experiment are useful for examining within-subjects effects of deception as well as across-occasion effects.

We fitted a linear mixed-effects model predicting statement detail using veracity as a fixed effect, with random intercepts and slopes for each participant and each phase of the interview (each corresponding to different activities the participant may have performed).
Overall, truthful and deceptive statements did not significantly differ in their level of detail, b = -1.68, 95% CI [-4.38, 1.03], t(4.10) = 1.21, p = .289.

However, there was considerable variation in the random intercepts and slopes for participants and interview phases (see Figure 2), such that baseline level of detail, as well as how the level of detail changed during deception, varied widely across both people and occasions.
text.formatted: However, there was considerable variation in the random intercepts and slopes for participants and interview phases (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>), such that baseline level of detail, as well as how the level of detail changed during deception, varied widely across both people and occasions.

text.text: Some people were much less detailed when they lied; for others, level of detail was unaffected by veracity.
These results indicate violations of the homogeneity requirement (Condition 1) and the stationarity requirement (Condition 2).
We see similar indications of non-ergodicity for other cues.

For instance, Calderon et al. (2022) synthesized transcriptions of truthful and deceptive statements from six experiments (total N = 528 people providing 6,104 messages; Kleinberg et al., 2017; Vrij, Granhag, et al., 2011; Vrij, Leal, et al., 2011; Warmelink, 2017; Warmelink et al., 2012 Warmelink et al., , 2013)).
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Calderon et al. (2022)</ref> synthesized transcriptions of truthful and deceptive statements from six experiments (total N = 528 people providing 6,104 messages; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kleinberg et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vrij, Granhag, et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vrij, Leal, et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Warmelink, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Warmelink et al., 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Warmelink et al., , 2013))</ref>.

text.text: In these data, truthful and deceptive messages differed only slightly on average in terms of word count (i.e., the total number of words the participant used when answering each question in an interview), such that deceptive statements tended to be longer than truthful statements, g = 0.08, 95% CI [0.02, 0.14].
However, this small average effect conceals the fact there were highly variable differences in word count between truthful and deceptive messages across the questions of the interviews (Figure 3).
text.formatted: However, this small average effect conceals the fact there were highly variable differences in word count between truthful and deceptive messages across the questions of the interviews (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Across questions, the difference in word count between true and deceptive statements varied widely, both in magnitude and direction.
For some questions, true statements were longer; for others, lies were longer.
This variation is greater than would be expected by sampling variation alone, Q (90) = 120.73, p = .017.
These results again indicate a violation of the stationarity requirement (Condition 2).
Analysis of data from Luke (2015, Study 2) Note.
Slopes and intercepts are unstandardized (one point on the scale indicates a change of one detail).
Negative slopes indicate that lies are less detailed than truths.
The Miami University Deception Detection Database (MU3D; Lloyd et al., 2019) includes recordings of N = 80 people each telling the truth twice and lying twice (a total of 320 messages).
text.formatted: The Miami University Deception Detection Database (MU3D; <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Lloyd et al., 2019)</ref> includes recordings of N = 80 people each telling the truth twice and lying twice (a total of 320 messages).

text.text: If we fit a linear mixed effects model predicting the length of each statement (word count), with the veracity of the message as a predictor and with random intercepts and slopes for each sender, we see that although veracity does not significantly predict word count on average, b = 1.763, t (79.002) = 0.897, p = .373, there is considerable variance in the random slopes for veracity across senders, SD = 6.717, range -8.35 to 7.09 (where positive values indicate longer statements when lying compared to telling the truth).
Put differently, some senders provide longer statements when lying compared to telling the truth, while the opposite is the case for others.
This variation violates the ergodicity requirement of homogeneity across individuals (Condition 1).
The situation is, in fact, even more complex when we examine how the effects of deception on word count systematically vary across other factors.

As can be seen in Figure 4, the effect varies across senders' average statement length when telling the truth, such that more verbose people (those who give longer truthful statements) tend to provide longer statements when lying compared to when they are telling the truth.
text.formatted: As can be seen in Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>, the effect varies across senders' average statement length when telling the truth, such that more verbose people (those who give longer truthful statements) tend to provide longer statements when lying compared to when they are telling the truth.

text.text: In contrast, less verbose people (i.e., those who tend to give shorter truthful statements) tend to give longer statements when they are telling the truth compared to when they are lying.
However, this relationship is further moderated such that it appears to vary between men and women.
In short, statement length varies as a function of veracity, but only for some people, and this variation is evidence against ergodicity. 2These results have important implications.
text.formatted: In short, statement length varies as a function of veracity, but only for some people, and this variation is evidence against ergodicity. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">2</ref>These results have important implications.

text.text: If the complexity of the patterns of variation we see here are representative of the kinds of systematic variation we would see for other cues to deception (and we see no reason to expect otherwise), group-level average effects are not equally poor representations of all individual-level effects, but they may be particularly poor representations for some groups of people.

If this is the case, inappropriately applying grouplevel conclusions to individuals will almost certainly have discriminatory effects in practical contexts (e.g., gender, ethnicity, and/or other individual differences), in patterns that are difficult or impossible to predict.

Similar concerns have been raised, for example, about deception detection techniques that impose cognitive load, which may have differential effects on people with higher or lower working memory capacity (Lane et al, 2014; Lane & Vieira, 2012; Maldonado et al, 2018).
text.formatted: Similar concerns have been raised, for example, about deception detection techniques that impose cognitive load, which may have differential effects on people with higher or lower working memory capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lane et al, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lane & Vieira, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Maldonado et al, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, practical recommendations about deception cues derived from group-level research (e.g., treating less detailed statements as more likely to be deceptive) will systematically disadvantage some groups and advantage others, while being ostensibly "scientific."

In sum, existing data provide compelling evidence that group-level models of the deception cues statement length and detail do not apply homogeneously across individuals and are not stationary across occasions.
We can think of no compelling arguments that other deception cues would not also fail to meet the two conditions of ergodicity.
Here, we have examined a limited set of the large body of datasets generated by deception researchers over the last century.
However, in every dataset we have looked at that has been suitable to test the assumptions of ergodicity, the assumptions have been clearly violated.
We have shown that deception cues are almost certainly non-ergodic.
Thus, the grouplevel conclusions from the previous century of deception cue research cannot be trusted to apply at the individual level.
To draw meaningful conclusions about deception cues and their underlying psychological processes, an individual-level research agenda must be adopted.
As an example, consider the common finding that many cues appear to have a nearzero association with deception at a group level (Luke, 2019).
text.formatted: As an example, consider the common finding that many cues appear to have a nearzero association with deception at a group level <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Luke, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, the analyses reported above suggest that the diagnostic value of a single cue may vary considerably across people and occasions.

The aggregate finding that a given cue is weakly associated with deception may be a poor description of many individuals: for some people the cue may be positively related to deception, for some people negatively, while others may show no relation at all.
Additionally, the relationships between cues may systematically vary across individuals (e.g., the same basic mental process might manifest with different behavioral indicators for different people).
Group-level analyses typically reported in deception research simply cannot uncover such insights.
To draw more meaningful conclusions, a repeated measures design with appropriate analyses is required.
Straightforward pervasiveness analyses (Speelman & McGann, 2026) show the value of adopting an individual-level approach.
text.formatted: Straightforward pervasiveness analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Speelman & McGann, 2026)</ref> show the value of adopting an individual-level approach.

text.text: These results suggest that a single explanatory mechanism is insufficient since those who provide longer statements when lying cannot be accounted for by the proposed theoretical explanation claiming that remembering is easier than fabrication.
In many cases a plurality of theoretical explanations may be required to best capture the pattern of deception cues at the individual level.
Further contributions to theory can come in the form of identifying general trends or "laws" at the individual level.
There is a common misconception that only group-level research can uncover generalizable laws of behavior.
However, through detailed research of individuals over time it is also possible to establish individual level laws, unlikely to be uncovered through group-level analysis (Robinson, 2011).

text.text: Famous examples of attempts to establish individuallevel laws in the history of psychology include Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve (Ebbinghaus, 1913; Radvansky et al., 2022; Rubin & Wenzel, 1996) and the principles of operant conditioning (Murphy & Lupfer, 2014; Staddon & Cerutti, 2003).

text.text: Operant conditioning provides an apt example of the potential insights that may be realized from an individual-level research agenda on deception cues.
According to operant conditioning, a positive reinforcer is a desired stimulus that, when presented after a behavior, will strengthen the behavior (Staddon & Cerutti, 2003).
text.formatted: According to operant conditioning, a positive reinforcer is a desired stimulus that, when presented after a behavior, will strengthen the behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Staddon & Cerutti, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: However, since people's preferences vary, what counts as a positive reinforcer will also vary between people.
For some people chocolate may be a positive reinforcer, for others, cigarettes.
Hence, although the general law is the same for all individuals, how it manifests at the individual level can look extremely different.
What if something similar occurs with deception cues?
Consider again the claim that lying is more cognitively demanding than truth telling (Blandón-Gitlin et al., 2014; Zuckerman et al., 1981; but see Neequaye, 2022).

text.text: Now consider the possibility that indicators of mental effort may vary between people.
When experiencing mental effort, some people may rub their chin; others may close their eyes.

If these individual differences are not taken into account, an analysis at the group level may result in near-zero associations between cues and deception, even if the general law that 'lying is more cognitively demanding than truth telling' is true.
Alternatively, group-level analyses may misleadingly suggest an association between some cues and deception on average, even if these relationships are complicated by person-level variation.
For example, imagine a situation where a cue has a strong relationship with deception for a small minority, but the same cue has no relationship with deception for the majority (as in Figure 5).

text.text: This pattern would produce a group-level effect indicating that, on average, the cue in question is a valid indicator of deception.

In a court case, judgments of whether a witness is lying do not concern witnesses in general, but one specific witness.
A customs officer questioning a suspected smuggler is not concerned about smugglers in general, but the specific person they are questioning.
An employer suspicious over claims in a CV, is not interested in CVs in general, but the specific CV they are assessing.

Non-ergodicity raises concerns about practical recommendations derived from group-level research on topics such as using checklists of verbal and nonverbal behavior to create composite scores of the likelihood of deception (Evans et al., 2013) or the use of the level of detail of a statement as an indicator of credibility (Verschuere et al., 2023).

text.text: Variance across individuals and occasions renders such recommendations potentially misleading, for at least some people and situations.
An individual-level research agenda will allow us to map the variances in patterns of deception cues across people and occasions.
This will increase our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of deception detection tools.
By identifying when, for whom, and why deception cues are valid, individual-level research can develop deception detection techniques that are more applicable to the individual case.

To provide a clearer sense of what exactly we are suggesting, it will be useful to sketch the contours of a possible individual-level research program, to provide some concrete examples of data collection paradigms, and to describe approaches to data analysis.

Some of what follows is common among all fields seeking to study phenomena at an individual level (e.g., the need to take multiple measures from individuals), but the unique features of the deception cue research require specific considerations. Luke (2019) has argued that one particularly methodologically problematic feature of the deception cue literature is that virtually any behavior that differs between truthful and deceptive messages in any direction and with any magnitude can be framed as theoretically interesting, and if using recorded material, researchers are able to code an unlimited number of behaviors from the raw data.

For this reason and others, we recommend an approach that encourages (if not requires) clear theoretical specification, to make hypotheses about mechanisms and cues explicit, without hampering the possibility of exploration (see, e.g., Guest & Martin, 2021).

text.text: How could an individual-level program of research on cues to deception proceed?
We propose four stages for such a program, focused on theory development and appraisal: 1.
Generation of a theoretical model of an underlying mechanism or mechanisms.
Identification of potential observable manifestations of the mechanism (i.e., potential deception cues related to the mechanism).
Empirical characterization of the individual variability in the identified cues as a function of the hypothesized mechanism 4.

Empirical characterization of the effect of deception on the hypothesized cues These stages should be understood as a rough outline, rather than a strict and linearly sequential process, but we have arranged the stages such that they build on each other and rely on information collected in previous stages.
Each stage also provides possibilities to make discoveries at each stage that falsify or set boundaries for the hypotheses under investigation.
Accordingly, the process must be iterative, with revisions to hypotheses necessitating revisitation to earlier stages.
If individual-level cues to deception exist (and we believe they probably do), the proposed process will be capable of providing a theoretically and empirically grounded description of them.
As a first step, a researcher should develop a theoretical account of a psychological (and/or physiological) mechanism thought to be causally related to deception.
That is, they should generate a causal model of psychological processes hypothesized to differ between the act of lying and telling the truth.

Several such models already exist (e.g., models that assert that lying is more cognitively demanding than telling the truth) but have, in our view, not been empirically assessed in a framework capable of actually testing them.

At this stage, it is important that researchers specify their theoretical models as explicitly and clearly as possible so that the hypothesis testing in subsequent stages can be oriented toward rigorously appraising Second, equipped with a theoretical account about a mechanism, the researcher can proceed to identify potential observable manifestations of the mechanism-that is, potential cues to deception related to the mechanism.
Such identification can proceed in a variety of ways, and in many cases, there is likely to be previous research from which potential cues can be derived.

Continuing with the theoretical claim that lying is more cognitively demanding than truth telling, researchers could, for example, use basic cognitive literature to identify measurable physiological and behavioral signs of heightened cognitive activity.
Third, the researcher should empirically characterize the individual variability in the identified cues as a function of the hypothesized mechanism.
At this stage, it is not necessary to study the cues in relation to deception.
Rather, the goal is to study the individual variability in the sensitivity and validity of the identified cues, across many people and under a variety of circumstances.

For example, if blink rate is identified in the second stage as an observable manifestation of cognitive load, the third stage can assess individual variability in blink rate to more direct manipulations of cognitive load.
This stage is primarily descriptive and exploratory, but it plays an important role in developing the foundation for informative hypothesis testing.
Basic empirical description of individual variability is invaluable for assessing the plausibility of deception-related hypotheses, as well as the practical demands of studying a given cue.

If it is found, for example, that the rate of blinking is related to cognitive load but that there is an enormous amount of individual variability in the extent to which cognitive activity affects the rate of blinking, these facts bear on the plausibility that and the generality with which deception might affect the rate of blinking.

As part of this process of characterizing individual variability, it is important to search for potential homogeneous subsets of individuals who may, for example, show diverging patterns of behavioral manifestations of the psychological mechanism under investigation (e.g., subgroups of people who reliably manifest cognitive load with different patterns of behavior).

Fourth and finally, the researcher should proceed to empirically characterize the effect of deception on the hypothesized cues, making special effort to sample across any subgroups identified at the third stage.
In contrast to earlier parts of the process, this stage is primarily aimed at hypothesis testing (though it does not preclude exploration).

Assessing the effects of deception with consideration to possible subgroups is crucial for correctly identifying for whom the hypothesis holds and in what ways (e.g., if different subgroups manifest different cues).
Importantly, at this stage (and all empirical stages of the research program), it is essential to take an approach to data collection that is suitable for individual-level analysis.

The basic approach for collecting data for individual-level research is a time series or repeated measures design, where the same individuals are repeatedly measured over a specified period, possibly under varying conditions (Barlow et al., 2009; Gregson, 1983; Molenaar & Campbell, 2009).

text.text: Taking several measures from the same person enables a direct assessment of intraindividual changes, as well as interindividual profile differences.

Though not common in deception cue research, this research design has a long history in psychology, in the domains of memory (Murre & Dros, 2015; Rubin & Wenzel, 1996), behaviorism (Carr & Durand, 1985; Morse & Skinner, 1958) and neuropsychology (Astafiev et al., 2004; Gryga et al., 2012; Olivo et al., 2022), among others.

text.text: We draw on these well-established research areas to inform our proposal for an individual-level approach to deception research.
Below we outline two experimental procedures to examine deception cues using a repeated measures design.

In the program outline above, these procedures are relevant to the fourth stage of the process, wherein a researcher may want to experimentally manipulate the veracity of messages to assess the effects of deception.

These suggested procedures are, of course, not intended to cover all possible approaches to individual-level deception research, but rather, are meant to serve as jumping-off points for a new paradigm and to illustrate the basic design features that might be desirable in laboratory research on deception.
The first approach is derived from the cue-word paradigm common in research on autobiographical memories (Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974; Harris et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The first approach is derived from the cue-word paradigm common in research on autobiographical memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Harris et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This highly controlled laboratorybased approach allows for greater reliability in measurement.
However, this greater experimental control reduces the realism of the setting.

To complement the cue-word paradigm, we also describe a design with a more interactive social context, since researchers have claimed that it is in the interaction of a dialogue that valid deception cues emerge (Burgoon & Buller, 1996).

text.text: This more interactive setup is based on the speed-dating paradigm that has previously been used in deception research (Falkiewicz et al., 2015).

text.text: These procedures represent two of many possible repeated measures designs to study cues to deceit.

These are certainly not meant as the final word, but rather as an introduction to the general methodological shift we propose and to inspire researchers to consider procedures that might be useful for collecting large amounts of repeated measures data.
In a typical cue-word study, each participant performs several trials.
In each trial participants are presented with a prompt-a word or phrase-and are required to briefly describe the first memory they recall in response to the prompt.
Each trial uses a different word, and participants will often perform 30+ trials (Barzykowski & Staugaard, 2016; Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974).
text.formatted: Each trial uses a different word, and participants will often perform 30+ trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barzykowski & Staugaard, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: This basic setup can be repurposed for a deception context by adding a within-subjects manipulation of veracity, resulting in honest trials and deceptive trials.
For honest trials, participants will honestly describe the autobiographical memories elicited by the prompts, as they would in a typical memory study.
For deceptive trials, participants will be required to lie by describing an event that they have not experienced.
This paradigm means that researchers can quite quickly and easily collect many true and false statements from the same participants.
This design is also highly flexible.
Depending on the goal of the research, the prompts can be changed to full sentences or phrased as questions.
The design is also scalable, both in terms of number of participants and the number of statements from each participant.
To properly examine intraindividual variation, people should be assessed a large number of times.
New problems of course come with a repeated measures design, including fatigue and training effects.
Fatigue can be mitigated by having sessions spread over days or weeks.
As for training effects, we do not necessarily see this as a problem.
Rather, we see it as another opportunity to gain new insights into deception cues.
If, for instance, it is the case that deception cues weaken after practice with a task, surely this is of utmost interest for both theoreticians and practitioners.
The second paradigm we propose is based on the speed-dating paradigm, introduced by Falkiewicz et al. (Falkiewicz et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The second paradigm we propose is based on the speed-dating paradigm, introduced by Falkiewicz et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Falkiewicz et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Participants are divided into pairs.
Pairs of participants will play a party game designed for strangers to become more acquainted with each other.
The game consists of cards, each of which contains one discussion topic concerning different personal information (e.g., music preferences).
Participants are to discuss each topic together for approximately one minute.
These one-minute discussions represent a trial.
For each trial, participants are randomly assigned to either discuss the topic honestly or deceitfully.
Crucially, for each topic, participants will be blind to whether their partner is telling the truth or lying.
As with the cue-word paradigm, this design is both flexible and scalable.
The discussion topics can easily be changed to suit the research goal.
For instance, if a researcher is interested in the interplay between emotion and deception, topics designed to elicit certain emotions, such as shame or embarrassment, could be used.
More complicated designs with confederates would also be possible, opening possibilities for investigating other research questions.
In terms of scalability, it is straightforward to increase the number of participants and the number of trials.
Past research on deception cues has used analytic techniques that have attempted to account for individual differences in different ways.

For example, researchers have examined how individual differences, such as personality, may moderate the diagnosticity of deception cues (Lee et al., 2008; Riggio & Friedman, 1983; Turi et al., 2022) or have used within-subjects analyses comparing individuals' behaviors when lying to their 'baseline' behavior when telling the truth (Bogaard et al., 2023; Verigin et al., 2021; Vrij, 2016).
text.formatted: For example, researchers have examined how individual differences, such as personality, may moderate the diagnosticity of deception cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lee et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Riggio & Friedman, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Turi et al., 2022)</ref> or have used within-subjects analyses comparing individuals' behaviors when lying to their 'baseline' behavior when telling the truth <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bogaard et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Verigin et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Vrij, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Although these analyses give an impression of an individual-level approach, they are still conducted at the group-level.
Ultimately, these analyses still focus on between-group differences and interindividual variation.
They do not, in any meaningful way, examine intraindividual variation required for a truly individual-level approach.
In fact, the lack of several measurements for each participant in most studies on deception cues means that an analysis of intraindividual variation is not possible at all.

Even in studies in which the same participants are assessed several times (as is the case in the data we examined above), conventional statistical approaches still do not provide insights on the individual level.
A methodological shift to an individual-level research agenda must move beyond the statistical techniques typically used.
One highly useful approach is based on network modeling (Fried & Cramer, 2017).

text.text: Network modeling is a flexible analytic approach that can be used to examine individual-level data, including data from panel designs and time-series designs (Epskamp, 2020).

text.text: One analytic technique that may be useful for deception researchers is Gaussian graphical modeling (GGM), which attempts to model the covariance structure of a set of variables (similar to structural equation modeling) as a sparse network of partial correlations.
An individual-level model can be constructed for each person, which provides measures of the association between each cue with deception, as well as with other cues.

Because edges in a GGM are partial correlations (accounting for shared variance of the variables in the model), observed associations between deception and a given cue are more plausibly direct causal relationships, compared to examining ordinary correlations.
For example, imagine a person for whom deception causes an increase in speech rate, which in turn increases speech errors.
In such a situation, there would be an apparent correlation between deception and speech errors, but this correlation would be mitigated or eliminated controlling for speech rate.
GGMs provide an efficient tool for implementing such statistical control.

In addition to being examined in themselves, individual network models can be combined to create an average group-level model, and a cross-sectional model across all messages can also be estimated (directly analogous to the method in group-level research).
Furthermore, the variability across individuals for each relationship can be modeled.
This variability model provides information about how much individuals differ, for example, in the extent to which different behaviors correlate with deception.
Using a variety of methods, clusters of interrelated cues can be identified (Blanken et al., 2018), both at the individual-and group-levels.
text.formatted: Using a variety of methods, clusters of interrelated cues can be identified <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Blanken et al., 2018)</ref>, both at the individual-and group-levels.

text.text: Examination of such clusters, as well as variability across individuals, can provide previously unavailable insight into the structure of deceptive behavior across people.

For instance, if we were to observe that many people feature one or more clusters of behavior that correlates with deception, even if the specific content of those clusters varies between people, we may be able to infer a general principle about the manner in which deception tends to influence behavior.

Network modeling is not the only quantitative approach one can take in order to examine phenomena on the individual level, but its flexibility, wide applicability to relevant situations in the deception literature, and the availability of software make it an appealing option.
Here we provide a worked example of a Network modelling approach of deception cues, using data from Loy et al. (2018).

text.text: In the study, 24 people each told 24 truths and 24 lies in an interactive context (total 1149 valid messages).
Each message was coded for several cues to deception.

Here, we examine 14 verbal and nonverbal cues from this dataset: filled pauses, silent pauses, substitutions, prolongations, repairs, repetitions, head movements, hand movements, body movements, shoulder movements, mouth movements, eyebrow movements, smiles, and gaze.
We used a network modeling approach to analyze the data.
Specifically, for each individual, we fit a Gaussian graphical model (GGM; Epskamp et al., 2018) using the psychonetrics package (Epskamp, 2021) for R (R Core Team, 2023).
text.formatted: Specifically, for each individual, we fit a Gaussian graphical model (GGM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Epskamp et al., 2018)</ref> using the psychonetrics package <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Epskamp, 2021)</ref> for R (R Core Team, 2023).

text.text: For each person, we found an optimal model by iteratively pruning and adding edges with a liberal alpha of .10, to minimize the Bayesian information criterion.
These personalized network models represent each individual's (within-subject) partial correlations between the measured behaviors and deception.
We also fit a GGM using the same approach across all messages by all individuals.
This cross-sectional network is akin to typical group-level deception research, as it represents the group-level partial correlations across messages.
Additionally, we estimated a network using person mean centered cue variables, to create a network representing the acrossindividual average (or average within-subjects effects).

One might expect the across-individual average network to be equivalent to the cross-sectional network, but under many circumstances the cross-sectional correlation and the average within-subjects correlation are not equal or even in the same direction (Hamaker, 2023).

text.text: Finally, we calculated the variance in the withinsubjects correlations for each possible edge in the full network, to depict the degree of variability across individuals.

For instance, one might hypothesize that speech disturbances (e.g., filled pauses, silent pauses, repairs) are indicative of a coherent psychological process involved in deception (e.g., the cognitive effort associated with fabrication).

Even if group-level analyses suggest positive correlations between these cues, the across-individual variance in the relationships between these cues suggests that these cues may not be consistent indicators across individuals.

It is by now almost a truism in the field that cues to deception are weak and unreliable.
Some have gone so far as to call research on deception cues a "blind alley" not worthy of future research (Brennen & Magnussen, 2020).
text.formatted: Some have gone so far as to call research on deception cues a "blind alley" not worthy of future research <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brennen & Magnussen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This conclusion is too sweeping.
The issue is not with research on deception cues, but rather the methodology and paradigm used to study them.
The typical group-level analysis only tells half the story (and indeed, this story is not favorable for offering practical recommendations).
What is needed to tell the other half is a methodological shift to an individual-level research agenda.

Although theoretical and meta-research discussions of deception acknowledge the difficulties in drawing conclusions about the individual from group averages (e.g., Brennen & Magnussen, 2022; Nahari, 2023), these discussions stop short of suggesting the overhaul of the methodological approach necessary to address this problem.

text.text: Our suggested shift to an individual-level research agenda would not amount to an amendment or extension of the approach that has dominated research on deception cues, but rather, it is a fundamentally different take on the topic.
One that we believe is required in order to progress research and theory in the field.
An individual-level approach will enable us to arrive at novel theoretical understandings of deception, from the bottom up.
We will be able to examine how, for example, deception may induce idiosyncratic changes in behavior in different cues (or clusters of cues) between individual people.

Understanding such potential differences can help provide crucial new insights into the psychological processes involved in human deception and create a science of people as individuals, rather than of averages across people.

Consider the networks for Participants 1 (leftmost on the top row of Figure7), 5 (second from the right on the top row), 6 (rightmost on the top row), and 7 (leftmost on the second row; larger versions of each network visualization are available in the online supplemental materials).
Participant 1 has an unconnected network, with no significant links between deception and any of the measured behaviors, though many of the cues are related to each other.
Participant 5 has a nearly fully connected network, with only one significant cue related to deception (i.e., silent pauses).
Participant 6 has a fully connected network, with three cues significantly related to deception (i.e., silent pauses, repairs, and eyebrow movements).
Participant 7's network is not fully connected, and they have only one cue significantly related to deception (i.e., silent pauses).
Notably, these participants had quite different individual-level cues to deception.
For instance, silent pauses were unrelated to deception for Participant 1, related negatively to deception for Participant 5, and positively related for Participants 6 and 7.
Each of these participants cue-to-cue relationships vary widely as well.
